Here excess means edges minus vertices. For a connected graph it is one less than the number of independent cycles. Deleting a leaf and its incident edge, or suppressing a degree-two vertex, preserves excess. This convention differs by one from the cyclomatic number for connected graphs.

A connected bicyclic graph has two independent cycles, equivalently excess one. Its 2-core has the same excess and every removed vertex lies in a tree attached to the core. The graph kernel captures the finite collection of possible branching structures.

Attach a forest with those core vertices as roots to obtain C(n,n+1)=∑k​(kn​)bk​knn−k−1. After division by nn+1 the relevant sum is n−2∑k​k3(n)k​/nk. Its upper bound follows from (n)k​/nk≤e−k(k−1)/(2n); its lower bound uses n​≤k≤2n​, where this product stays bounded below. The sum is bounded above and below by positive constants. Bicyclic kernel classification

Words: 77
Bicyclic graph OurBigBook.com
The graph kernel of a bicyclic graph satisfies ∑v​(degv−2)=2, with all degrees at least three. It therefore has either one degree-four vertex carrying two loops, a bouquet graph, or two degree-three vertices. In the latter case connectivity and degree counting give either three parallel edges, the three-edge Theta graph, or one edge between the vertices and one loop at each, a dumbbell graph. All bicyclic cores are subdivisions of these three kernels, subject to simplicity restrictions on loop lengths and parallel paths.

2-core of a graph (C2​(G))

Words: 123 Articles: 1
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The 2-core is the unique largest induced subgraph with minimum degree at least two. It is obtained by repeatedly deleting vertices of degree zero or one. Every subgraph with minimum degree two survives each deletion, which proves maximality and order independence. In a connected graph with a nonempty 2-core, the deleted vertices form rooted trees attached individually to the core vertices.

Graph kernel (K(G))

Words: 67
2-core of a graph OurBigBook.com
For a connected graph whose 2-core contains a vertex of degree at least three, suppress each maximal path with degree-two internal vertices to a single edge, allowing its two endpoints to coincide. The resulting multigraph, retaining loops and parallel edges, is its kernel. Suppression preserves graph excess and leaves minimum degree at least three. A purely cyclic core is a separate unicyclic case; it has no branching vertex to anchor this construction.

Chordal graph

Words: 137 Articles: 2
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A chordal graph is an undirected graph in which every cycle of length at least four has a chord. Its structure allows exact junction tree calculations using its maximal cliques.

Triangulation of an undirected graph

Words: 52
Chordal graph OurBigBook.com
Triangulation adds fill edges to an undirected graph to make it a chordal graph. Given an elimination ordering, join all remaining neighbors of each removed vertex. The completed graph has that perfect elimination ordering. Fill edges can enlarge the cliques used for exact probabilistic graphical model inference, without changing the original probability factors; they do not assert new biological relationships.

Perfect elimination ordering

Words: 59
Chordal graph OurBigBook.com
A perfect elimination ordering successively removes a graph vertex whose remaining neighbors form a clique. An undirected graph is a chordal graph exactly when it has such an ordering. In one direction, the earliest vertex of an induced long cycle would have two nonadjacent later neighbors, contradicting the ordering. The converse follows by the existence of a simplicial vertex in every finite chordal graph.

Johnson graph (J(n,k))

Words: 242 Articles: 2
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The Johnson graph has the k-element subsets of an n-element set as vertices, with two vertices adjacent exactly when their intersection has k−1 elements. Relabelling the ground set gives graph automorphisms. The maximal cliques of a Johnson graph allow reconstruction of those ground-set labels when the two clique sizes are different.

Distance in a Johnson graph (d(A,B)=k−∣A∩B∣)

Words: 65
Johnson graph OurBigBook.com
One edge of a Johnson graph replaces one element of a k-subset, so it can increase intersection with a fixed target by at most one. Replacing each element outside the target by one missing target element gives a path reaching this lower bound. Equal-distance ordered pairs have equal sizes of intersection, the two differences and the remaining ground set; a permutation matching these four regions proves distance transitivity.

Maximal cliques of a Johnson graph (n−k+1andk+1)

Words: 130
Johnson graph OurBigBook.com
For 1<k<n−1, the maximal cliques of J(n,k) are the families containing a fixed (k−1)-subset, of size n−k+1, and the families contained in a fixed (k+1)-subset, of size k+1. To see why these exhaust the possibilities, write two adjacent vertices as D∪{a} and D∪{b}. A common adjacent vertex either contains D or lies in D∪{a,b}. A vertex of the first kind outside that union is not adjacent to a vertex of the second kind omitting an element of D, so a clique cannot mix these alternatives. For J(n,3) and n≥5, n=6, the clique sizes n−2 and four distinguish the families containing pairs. Their incidence recovers J(n,2), whose stars of size n−1 distinguish the individual ground-set points from its triangular cliques.

Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The maximum degree of a finite graph is the largest number of edges incident to one vertex. A bound d on degree bounds the number of vertices within distance k of a fixed vertex by 1+d+⋯+dk. Such counting bounds turn a large vertex count into a lower bound on diameter.

For a simple graph, let rij​ count the common neighbours of vertices i,j. Choosing two such neighbours makes a four-cycle, and each cycle is counted twice through its opposite pairs. The displayed identity follows even when extra edges are present, since cycles are counted as subgraphs rather than induced subgraphs. Also ∑i<j​rij​=∑v​(2d(v)​). Applying Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to degrees and Jensen inequality to common-neighbour counts gives extremal edge and cycle bounds.

Shortest path problem (minp:s⇝t​∑e∈p​we​)

Words: 358 Articles: 5
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A shortest path minimizes the sum of edge lengths between two vertices. With nonnegative lengths, a shortest walk can be reduced to a simple path by removing cycles, so exponentially many candidate paths can be searched implicitly. The Dijkstra algorithm solves this problem in polynomial time.

Label-setting shortest-path algorithm

Words: 62
Shortest path problem OurBigBook.com
An algorithm that makes each vertex's distance permanent once it is selected. With nonnegative directed edge lengths, the Dijkstra algorithm selects the unfinalized vertex with least tentative distance; a shorter route through another unfinalized vertex is impossible because its remaining route has at least that next tentative distance. For an all-to-one problem, incoming directed edges to the selected vertex are relaxed. Negative lengths can invalidate this finalization argument.

Bellman inequalities (di​≤cij​+dj​)

Words: 62
Shortest path problem OurBigBook.com
For an all-to-one shortest path problem with root r and dr​=0, these inequalities ensure that di​ is no larger than any directed path length from i to r, by summing along that directed path. If every finite di​ is also the length of a discovered directed path, the inequalities certify exact shortest-path labels. Nodes from which the root is unreachable retain infinite distance and are handled separately.

Label-correcting shortest-path algorithm

Words: 52
Shortest path problem OurBigBook.com
An algorithm whose tentative distance labels may be revised repeatedly until all relevant Bellman inequalities hold. Bellman-Ford algorithm uses this approach: a label is an upper bound supplied by a discovered directed path, and relaxing an directed edge can replace it with a shorter discovered directed path. A finite label is not declared permanent merely because it has been processed.

Bellman-Ford algorithm

Words: 71
Shortest path problem OurBigBook.com
For an all-to-one shortest path problem with root r, initialize dr(0)​=0 and all other labels to infinity. Set di(k)​=min(di(k−1)​,min(i,j)∈A​{cij​+dj(k−1)​}), keeping the root at zero. Induction identifies the labels with the shortest directed paths using at most k directed edges. Without a reachable negative directed cycle, ∣V∣−1 rounds suffice after removing directed cycles from a shortest walk. In-place or queue variants repeatedly relax incoming directed edges to an improved label. Labels may decrease multiple times, so this is a label-correcting shortest-path algorithm.

Dijkstra algorithm

Words: 68
Shortest path problem OurBigBook.com
Starting with distance zero at the source and infinity elsewhere, repeatedly finalize the unfinalized vertex with least tentative distance and relax its outgoing edges. Nonnegative lengths ensure that no later path can improve a finalized distance: any alternative path first reaches an unfinalized vertex whose tentative distance is at least the finalized one. A binary heap gives O((∣V∣+∣E∣)log∣V∣) arithmetic operations, and storing predecessors recovers a minimizing path.

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A graph minor is obtained by deleting vertices, deleting edges, and performing edge contractions. Equivalently, its vertices can be represented by disjoint nonempty connected sets of vertices in the original graph, with an edge joining two sets whenever the corresponding vertices are adjacent. These are branch sets of a graph minor.

Rooted branch-set reduction (m=h−q/2)

Words: 892
Graph minor OurBigBook.com
Let q≥2 be even, let S={x1​,…,xq​}, and suppose a graph has h disjoint nonempty vertex sets C1​,…,Ch​, where h≥d+3q/2. Suppose each G[Ci​] is connected or every one of its graph components meets S, and each Ci​ is adjacent to all but at most d of the other Cj​ not meeting S. Assume also that no rooted separation of a graph of order below q avoids d+1 of these sets. Then there are m=h−q/2 disjoint connected vertex sets D1​,…,Dm​ such that xi​∈Di​ for 1≤i≤q and each of these first q sets is adjacent to all but at most d of Dq+1​,…,Dm​.
Here adjacency of sets means existence of an edge between them. A rooted separation of a graph is (A,B) with A∪B=V(G), S⊆A, no edges between A∖B and B∖A, and order ∣A∩B∣. It avoids Ci​ when A∩Ci​=∅. We prove the reduction by induction, first on the vertex count and then on the edge count; any counterexample chosen minimal in this ordering will be impossible.
We may delete edges joining two vertices of S. They cannot affect rooted separations of a graph, since S lies wholly on the first side. Within a branch set, their deletion can only split a graph component into graph components each containing an endpoint in S, so the branch-set hypothesis also persists. An isolated vertex outside S and all branch sets can be deleted. An isolated vertex v∈S is also impossible, since (S,V(G)∖{v}) has order q−1 and avoids at least h−q≥d+q/2≥d+1 sets. Thus in a minimal counterexample S is independent, and every isolated vertex outside S belongs to a singleton branch set.
Consider a rooted separation of a graph (A,B) of order exactly q avoiding at least d+1 branch sets, and put S′=A∩B. Restrict to G′=G[B]−E(G[S′]) and Ci′​=Ci​∩B. Each Ci′​ is nonempty: any Ci​ not itself avoided is adjacent to at least one of the d+1 avoided sets, and the endpoint of such an edge in Ci​ must lie in B. If a graph component of G′[Ci′​] misses S′, it lies in B∖A and is a whole graph component of G[Ci​], with no vertex of S. The original hypothesis then forces G[Ci​] to be connected and Ci′​=Ci​, entirely outside A. Thus each restricted set is connected or all its graph components meet S′. In particular every Cj′​ missing S′ equals an original set outside A, so all its required adjacencies from Ci′​ persist.
A rooted separation of a graph (A′,B′) of G′ avoiding d+1 restricted sets lifts to (A∪A′,B′) in G, of the same order: an avoided restricted set misses S′, hence is an original set outside A. The edges removed inside S′ do not obstruct lifting, since S′⊆A′. This proves the required separation hypothesis for G′. If G′ is smaller, induction gives the desired connected sets rooted at S′. Moreover G[A] has q disjoint graph paths from S to S′, by the Menger theorem. Indeed a separator of smaller order between these sets would give a rooted separation of a graph of G of smaller order still avoiding those d+1 original sets. Truncate the graph paths at their first visits to S′, label their endpoints accordingly, and adjoin each graph path to the corresponding rooted connected set. They meet B only in their distinct endpoints, so this gives the desired sets for G, a contradiction. Consequently in a minimal counterexample every such separation of order q has B=V(G) and A=S, an independent set.
Now contract any edge whose endpoints do not belong to two different branch sets. Its endpoints cannot both lie in S, so the image of S still has size q. The branch-set conditions persist. If the contraction created a forbidden rooted separation of a graph of order below q, its lift would have order below q, except possibly when the contracted vertex lies in its separator. In that case the lifted order increases by one and is at most q. Equality would put the contracted edge inside A, contradicting the just-proved independence of A for an order-q separation avoiding d+1 sets. Thus the separation hypothesis also persists. Applying induction in the contracted graph and expanding the contracted vertex would produce the required disjoint connected sets. Hence every edge in a minimal counterexample joins two different branch sets.
Every vertex outside the branch sets would be isolated, since every edge joins two branch sets; such an isolated vertex could be deleted. Thus the branch sets cover the graph. Each nonsingleton branch set is therefore an independent set, and all its vertices belong to S, because each of its singleton graph components must meet S. Let C be the union of the nonsingleton branch sets, and write c=∣C∣≤q. There is a matching in a graph from C into V(G)∖S. Otherwise the Hall marriage theorem gives X⊆C with neighbourhood Y⊆V(G)∖S satisfying ∣Y∣<∣X∣. Since S is independent, (S∪Y,V(G)∖X) is a rooted separation of a graph of order q−∣X∣+∣Y∣<q. It avoids every singleton branch set outside S∪Y, of which there are at least
∣V(G)∣−q−∣Y∣≥∣V(G)∣−q−c+1≥h−2c​−q+1≥h−23q​+1≥d+1.
(1)
The penultimate counting bound uses that the nonsingleton sets number at most c/2, so ∣V(G)∣−c≥h−c/2. This contradicts the separation hypothesis.
Use that matching in a graph to make a two-vertex connected set for each terminal in C; terminals outside C remain singleton sets. There are at least
∣V(G)∣−q−c≥h−23q​=m−q
(2)
unused vertices, all singleton original branch sets. Choose m−q of them for the remaining Di​. Every rooted Di​ contains a singleton original branch set: either its terminal, or its terminal's matched neighbour. That singleton misses at most d of the selected nonterminal singleton sets. This constructs the desired family and completes the proof.

Random branch-set construction of a complete graph minor

Words: 74
Branch set of a graph minor OurBigBook.com
In a dense graph with many common neighbours for every pair of vertices, choose disjoint random small sets. A set is good if few vertices have no neighbour in it. Add unused common neighbours to connect each set and to repair the remaining missing adjacencies. Semi-random palette refinement for triangle-free colouring

Words: 80

Maintain lists of available colours, tentatively colour small random portions, erase conflicts and prune colours used by neighbours. In a triangle-free graph, a vertex's neighbours form an independent set, which enables local estimates. Track list size and average remaining neighbour congestion per colour; prune unusually congested colours before the next round. Concentration and the Lovász local lemma preserve these invariants until lists have enough slack for completion. Tracking averages matters because triangle-free graphs can still contain many four-cycles and need not have uniform per-colour congestion.

If each neighbourhood misses a fixed positive fraction of the possible pairs at a large degree bound, randomly assign about half that many colours and erase vertices with monochromatic incident edges. A nonadjacent neighbour pair can share a retained colour, giving a neighbour-colour saving. Write the number of successful repeated colours as a difference of two certifiable functions: colours with a nonadjacent pair, minus those for which a neighbour loses that colour. Both change by at most two under one-coordinate changes and have constant-size certificates. Talagrand's convex distance inequality and the Lovász local lemma make their linear expected saving simultaneous at all high-degree vertices; low-degree vertices have slack already. This yields a colouring using a fixed positive fraction fewer than the degree bound.

When t has colour T and the inputs x,y,z have colours in {T,F}, this graph admits an extension to a graph colouring with three colours exactly when at least one input is T. All-false inputs force a=d=F, contradicting their edge. Conversely, use (a,b,c,d,e)=(T,F,B,F,B) if x=T, (T,B,F,F,B) if x=F,y=T, and (F,T,B,B,F) if x=y=F,z=T. For a graph whose vertices are partitioned into parts, an independent transversal is an independent set containing exactly one vertex from each part. Route each game-node flow to one of its two teams, and cap the team's total additional wins at W−wi​−1 for a strict target victory. A negative cap immediately rules out success. Otherwise an integral maximum flow saturating every game-source arc specifies the winners of all games and proves feasibility. Each actual game is counted once; duplicating ordered pairs changes the problem.

Every finite planar graph admits a proper vertex coloring with at most five colors. Euler formula for a connected planar graph supplies a vertex of degree at most five. If they are connected, planarity prevents opposite neighbours 2 and 4 from being connected in their two-color subgraph, and that interchange frees a color instead. This is a Kempe chain proof.

There are at most as many proposals as edges, so this terminates. A rejected proposer can never become preferable to the receiver's final partner, since the receiver's held partner only improves. An edge never proposed along cannot block either: its proposer finishes with a better partner or has exhausted all choices. Thus the final matching in a graph is stable.

A Cayley formula upper bound for connected sets excludes component sizes k+1 through a small fixed fraction of n; the empty-graph cut bound excludes the remaining sizes up to n/2. An extra-edge count excludes cyclic small graph components. The expected value of the number of vertices in small nonisolated tree components is O(nde−2d)=o(ne−d), where d=np. The Markov inequality completes the count of vertices outside the unique large graph component.

Breadth-first exploration of a binomial random graph (Ut​=(1−p)(Ut−1​−bt​)−Dt​)

Words: 93
Erdős-Rényi model OurBigBook.com
During Breadth-first search of G(n,p) let Ut​ count unseen vertices, At​ active vertices, and t explored vertices. When At−1​=0 start a new unseen root, recorded by bt​=1; otherwise bt​=0. The newly discovered count is conditionally Bin(Ut−1​−bt​,p). Subtract its conditional mean to obtain a martingale difference Dt​. With q=1−p, U0​=n and A0​=0, iteration gives
At​=n−t−nqt+∑j≤t​qt−j+1bj​+qt∑j≤t​q−jDj​.
(56)
The last sum is a martingale. Positive At​ over an interval means that the graph component under exploration does not finish there. Independently adding phantom children couples each component exploration below a binomial branching process with offspring law Bin(n,p).

Uniform random graph process (Gn,m​)

Words: 241 Articles: 2
Erdős-Rényi model OurBigBook.com
Start with the empty graph and reveal the edges of the complete graph in a uniformly random order. After m steps its edge set is a uniform m-element subset. Independent uniform edge labels couple this process with all binomial random graphs: G(n,p)=Gn,M(p)​, where M(p) has a binomial distribution with parameters (2n​),p. For a monotone graph property, concentration of M(p) transfers a threshold estimate between edge probability and edge count.
Connectivity hitting time equals disappearance of isolated vertices (τconn​=τδ≥1​ with high probability)
Words: 103
Uniform random graph process OurBigBook.com
Couple the process with independent uniform edge labels, and expose p−​=(logn−41​loglogn)/n. A spanning-tree union bound excludes components of orders 2 through n/logn, and a cut bound excludes orders up to n/2. The graph has one large component and at most logn isolated vertices, with at least one isolated vertex. Before p+​=(logn+41​loglogn)/n, the probability of any new edge between those isolated vertices is O((logn)2loglogn/n)=o(1). All have joined the large component by p+​ by the isolated-vertex threshold in the Erdős-Rényi model. Throughout this window the only obstruction to connectivity is an isolated vertex, establishing the equality of hitting times.
Marked-set connectivity threshold (τL​∼41​nlogn(∣L∣∼n​))
Words: 75
Uniform random graph process OurBigBook.com
For a fixed set L of ⌊n​⌋ vertices, let τL​ be the first step at which they all belong to one graph component. In the uniform random graph process, τL​ lies between n(logn−ω)/4 and n(logn+ω)/4 with high probability for every ω→∞. Below that scale the marked isolated vertex count has divergent expected value and small relative variance. Above it the logarithmic-regime giant component misses o(n​) vertices; exchangeability and a union bound show that none are marked. The label coupling then transfers the two assertions to the process.

Tree-component expectation in the Erdős-Rényi model (EXj​=(jn​)jj−2pj−1(1−p)j(n−j)+(2j​)−j+1)

Words: 166 Articles: 1
Erdős-Rényi model OurBigBook.com
For Xj​ the number of tree components of order j in a binomial random graph, choose their vertices, choose one of jj−2 labelled trees by the Cayley formula, require its j−1 edges, and exclude both the remaining internal edges and all crossing edges. For j=1 interpret jj−2=1, recovering the isolated vertex count. If p=λ/n for fixed positive λ and j=O(logn), the Stirling formula gives EXj​∼n(λe1−λ)j/(λ2π​j5/2). Distinct overlapping vertex sets cannot both be graph components; for disjoint sets their joint occurrence gains the factor (1−p)−j2 relative to the product, because their between-set edges must be absent only once.
Fixed-order tree-component window (ωn−k/(k−1)≤p≤[logn+(k−1)loglogn−ω]/(kn))
Words: 75
Tree-component expectation in the Erdős-Rényi model OurBigBook.com
For fixed k≥2 and ω→∞, the expected number of tree components of order k is asymptotic to kk−2nkpk−1e−knp/k! throughout the displayed window. It tends to infinity: split np at 1 and (logn)/(2k) to obtain lower bounds of orders ωk−1, n​, and eω. Distinct overlapping vertex sets cannot both be components; disjoint sets have joint-to-product probability ratio (1−p)−k2=1+o(1). Thus the relative variance vanishes, proving a component of order k exists with high probability.

Assign an independent uniform label Ue​ to every possible edge and include e in G(n,p) exactly when Ue​≤p. This couples all edge probabilities so that p≤q implies G(n,p)⊆G(n,q).

1−p=∏i=1k​(1−pi​).

Connectivity threshold in the Erdős-Rényi model OurBigBook.com
A disconnected binomial random graph has a connected component of a graph with at most half its vertices. The union bound over its possible vertex sets gives
Pr(G(n,p) disconnected)≤∑s=1⌊n/2⌋​(sn​)(1−p)s(n−s)≤∑s=1⌊n/2⌋​(n(1−p)n/2)s.

Critical-window connectivity probability of a binomial random graph (P(G(n,(logn+c)/n) is connected)→e−e−c)
Words: 54
Connectivity threshold in the Erdős-Rényi model OurBigBook.com
For fixed real c, the number of isolated vertices in a binomial random graph with p=(logn+c)/n converges to a Poisson distribution of mean e−c. Its fixed factorial moments tend to (e−c)k. A union bound for small connected components, together with exclusion of intermediate components, shows that isolated vertices are asymptotically the only obstruction to connectivity. Thus the displayed limit is the zero-mass of that Poisson distribution.

Sparse clique-count concentration

For p=n−2/3logn, the number X of copies of K4​ satisfies
EX=(4n​)p6∼24(logn)6​

and var(X)=o((EX)2). Two distinct copies have dependent indicators only when they share at least two vertices; pairs sharing two or three vertices contribute respectively O(n6p11) and O(n5p9) to the variance.
Pendant extensions of sparse clique copies
Words: 85
Sparse clique-count concentration OurBigBook.com
If H is formed by attaching one pendant edge to a fixed clique, each copy has a unique clique core. Its number of extensions is the number of ambient edges from that core to outside vertices. At a scale where the core count is tight and its expected extension count diverges sufficiently rapidly, a Chernoff bound uniformly over all possible cores shows that the total count, divided by the extension mean, has the same limiting law as the core count. Non-induced copies are intended; extra ambient edges are not forbidden.

(65)
Thus, with probability tending to one, all the K4​ copies are vertex-disjoint. Together with sparse clique-count concentration, this gives arbitrarily many vertex-disjoint copies with probability tending to one.

Complement graph

Words: 78 Articles: 1
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The complement of a simple graph has exactly the edges absent from the original graph; a vertex of degree d acquires degree n−1−d.

Simultaneously bipartite graph and complement

Words: 54
Complement graph OurBigBook.com
If a graph and its complement graph are both bipartite, then the graph has at most four vertices. Indeed, each part of a bipartition of the original graph induces a clique in the complement and therefore has at most two vertices. The bound is attained by the four-vertex path, whose complement is another four-vertex path.

Menger theorem

Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The maximum number of disjoint paths joining two vertex sets equals the minimum size of a separating set, with vertex and edge versions according to the chosen notion of disjointness.

Vertex separator

Words: 26

An x-y vertex separator is a set of vertices, excluding x and y, whose deletion leaves no path from x to y.

Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
For nonadjacent vertices a,b of a graph G, their local connectivity κ(a,b;G) is the minimum size of an a-b vertex separator. By the Menger theorem, it also equals the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint a-b paths.

Internally vertex-disjoint paths

Words: 13
Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
Paths with common endpoints are internally vertex-disjoint when they share no other vertex.

Set version of Menger theorem

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
For vertex sets A,B, the maximum number of pairwise vertex-disjoint A-B paths equals the minimum size of a vertex set meeting every A-B path.

Fan lemma

Words: 46
Set version of Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
In a k-connected graph, for a vertex x and a set Y of at least k other vertices, there are k paths from x to distinct vertices of Y that meet only at x. This follows from the Set version of Menger theorem by separating x from Y.

Linked graph

Words: 218 Articles: 2
Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
A graph is k-linked when any 2k distinct vertices paired as (xi​,yi​) can be joined by k mutually vertex-disjoint paths from xi​ to yi​.
Unlike vertex connectivity, linkage specifies all endpoint pairings simultaneously.

Four-connected planar obstruction to two-linkage

Words: 87
Linked graph OurBigBook.com
On vertices 0,…,7, join cyclic indices differing by one or two modulo eight. The resulting planar graph has a square face bounded in order by 0,2,4,6. Deleting at most three vertices cannot disconnect it: each break in the surviving cyclic chain requires two consecutive deleted vertices, and two separate breaks require four deletions. It is therefore four-connected. Disjoint paths joining 0 to 4 and 2 to 6 would cross in the complementary disk of the square face, contrary to the Jordan curve theorem. Thus four-connectivity does not guarantee two-linkage.

Rooted dense minor linkage (2δ(H)≥∣H∣+4k−1)

Words: 97
Linked graph OurBigBook.com
If a graph is 2k-connected and has a graph minor H satisfying 2δ(H)≥∣H∣+4k−1, it is k-linked. Write d=∣H∣−1−δ(H), so ∣H∣≥2d+4k+1. The rooted branch-set reduction replaces the minor model by ∣H∣−k disjoint connected sets, the first 2k containing any prescribed terminals separately, each missing at most d of the remaining sets. Every prescribed pair then has at least k+1 common adjacent unused sets, allowing the k connections to be selected successively. The reduction uses rooted separations of a graph, contraction of edges outside distinct branch sets, and a final Hall marriage theorem matching; the separation condition prevents a contraction from destroying access to the model.

Rooted separation of a graph

Words: 77
Vertex connectivity OurBigBook.com
For a specified set S of vertices, a rooted separation is a pair (A,B) with A∪B=V(G), S⊆A, and no edges between A∖B and B∖A. Its order is ∣A∩B∣. It avoids a branch set C when A∩C=∅. A graph with vertex connectivity at least ∣S∣ has no rooted separation of order below ∣S∣ avoiding a nonempty branch set: both sides of such a separation would be nonempty after deleting its separator.

A TKr​ is a subdivision of the complete graph Kr​. Its original complete-graph vertices are branch vertices and its replaced edges are branch paths.

König's theorem equates the minimum vertex-cover size of a bipartite graph with its maximum matching size.

Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The Erdős-Gallai theorem characterizes which finite nonincreasing sequences of nonnegative integers form the degree sequence of a simple graph, using an even total degree and partial-sum inequalities.

A prism graph joins two copies of a cycle graph by matching corresponding vertices. The triangular prism graph is the three-cycle case, with six vertices and nine edges.

Squaregraph

Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A squaregraph has a plane embedding in which every bounded face has four sides and every interior vertex has degree at least four. Its outer face may have more than four sides, so this definition differs from a planar quadrangulation requiring every face to have degree four.

Vertex cycle cover

Words: 29
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A vertex cycle cover is a collection of cycles whose union contains every vertex of a graph; its cycles can overlap. A cycle cover of a directed graph additionally requires directed, vertex-disjoint cycles, and a spanning circuit family can allow overlaps.

Pósa's theorem

Words: 26
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
Pósa's theorem gives a sufficient degree-sequence condition for a Hamiltonian cycle in a finite simple graph. Longest-path rotation is a technique used in proving Hamiltonicity results; it is not itself the degree-sequence theorem.

Pseudoforest

Words: 39
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A pseudoforest is an undirected graph in which every connected component of a graph contains at most one cycle in a graph. Thus each component is a tree or a unicyclic component. A finite tree component has one fewer edge than vertices; a finite unicyclic component has equally many edges and vertices.
